analysis.one_liner: Taxes half of big oil companies' windfall profits and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2023, it sat there until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large oil companies an extra tax equal to half the amount that crude oil prices exceed their 2015-2019 average price. Only companies that extract or import more than 300,000 barrels a day would pay. All the money collected would go into a fund and be rebated to individual taxpayers, with the rebate phased out for households earning over $150,000 (joint) or $75,000 (single). It applied retroactively to 2022, when oil and gasoline prices spiked after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers below the income phase-out thresholds — most Americans — would receive a refundable credit funded entirely by the oil tax, with larger amounts on joint returns. The credit phases down for households above $150,000 (joint), $112,500 (head of household), or $75,000 (single) [S3]. The CRS summary describes the same design: an excise tax on windfall crude oil profits, with rebates paid to individual taxpayers from a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted or imported by companies averaging over 300,000 barrels a day, equal to half the amount that the quarterly average Brent crude price exceeds its inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average — targeting profits from the 2022 price spike rather than ordinary operations [S3].

All tax revenue is deposited in a dedicated 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and paid out as refundable income-tax credits to individual taxpayers, with joint filers receiving 150% of the base amount and the credit fully refundable so non-taxpayers can claim it [S3].
The credit phases out only above $150,000 of income for joint returns and $75,000 for others, meaning the benefit flows to most working households rather than to high earners [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large integrated oil producers and importers — companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels of crude a day, which describes the major integrated companies and large independents. Smaller producers are exempt. To the extent companies pass the tax through, some of the cost could surface in gasoline prices at the pump, and the tax could reduce incentives to expand supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large crude oil producers and importers

drawbacks.text: An excise tax tied to world oil prices could be passed through to consumers at the pump and could discourage investment in additional oil supply, which would tend to raise prices over time — a concern critics of windfall profits taxes raised about similar proposals [S3].

The tax is triggered by comparing current Brent crude prices to an inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average, a benchmark set partly by a period of unusually low oil prices, so it activates even in ordinary price environments once inflation adjustments accrue [S3].

Rebates are fixed dollar amounts divided among eligible individuals by the Treasury, so they are not calibrated to each household's actual gasoline spending — heavy drivers get the same rebate as light ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households below the phase-out, the design is a direct transfer: oil profits above a historical benchmark are taxed and the money is mailed back to taxpayers. The main good-faith objection is that taxing windfall production could shrink future supply and nudge pump prices up, partially offsetting the rebate — a trade-off the bill's supporters accepted in favor of clawing back excess 2022 profits. The design is simple but blunt: the rebate is flat rather than tied to driving, and the benchmark adjusts for inflation automatically rather than to actual costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 14, 2023, with 18 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and 1 Independent [S1][S4][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or hearing, and the bill never reached the Senate floor during the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large crude oil producers and importers, which would have paid the tax; taxpayers never received the rebates it would have funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil companies that never paid the tax

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Big Oil Windfall Profits Tax Act and assembled 18 cosponsors for it

for.name: Democratic cosponsors (17 Democrats and Sen. Bernie Sanders)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill its only demonstrated support; no Republican signed on

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on February 14, 2023 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it; the bill received no further action after referral [S5]

against.name: Senate Republican Conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator sponsored or cosponsored the bill, leaving it without a path to the 60 votes typically needed to advance a tax bill through the Senate

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or allied Independent — 18 total out of 51 Democratic-caucus senators — and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers
industries.note: Companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels a day would pay 50% of the excess of Brent prices over their 2015-2019 average on every barrel. Because the tax was never enacted, these companies kept the windfall profits it targeted.

industries.industry: Smaller independent oil and gas producers
industries.note: The tax exempts companies below the 300,000-barrel-per-day threshold, so smaller producers would face no new tax while their larger competitors did. This carve-out limits the bill to the biggest integrated players.
Not an industry, but the bill's whole payout side: tax proceeds flow to individual taxpayers as refundable credits, phased out only above $150,000 (joint) or $75,000 (single) in income.
